summary: Describes extensions to RSVP-TE for setting up traffic-engineered point-to-multipoint label switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks. The approach relies on RSVP-TE alone and does not need a multicast routing protocol in the provider core. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4875 extends RSVP-TE so one traffic-engineered label-switched path can reach several destinations. Routers at branches copy the incoming labeled data onto the outgoing paths for those destinations.

questions: how to set up p2mp te lsps
how does p2mp lsp grafting and pruning work
subtitle: How RSVP-TE signals traffic-engineered paths from one sender to many receivers.

tldr.problem: Earlier RSVP-TE specifications established point-to-point traffic-engineered paths, but did not define how to set up a point-to-multipoint LSP.
tldr.mechanism: A P2MP LSP groups source-to-leaf sub-LSPs under a shared session. Path messages describe destinations and routes, while branch LSRs replicate labeled data onto outgoing interfaces.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4875 defines setup, updates, pruning, rerouting, and protection for P2MP TE LSPs without requiring a multicast routing protocol in the provider core. RFC 6510 later updates it.

today: RFC 4875 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6510.

sections.title: From Point-to-Point Paths to a Tree
sections.content:
RFC 3209 defines RSVP-TE for point-to-point traffic-engineered LSPs, and RFC 3473 extends it for GMPLS. Those documents do not define point-to-multipoint (P2MP) LSPs. RFC 4875 adds signaling to establish them in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

A P2MP LSP consists of source-to-leaf (S2L) sub-LSPs between an ingress LSR and egress LSRs. At a branch LSR, incoming labeled data is replicated onto one or more outgoing interfaces, which may use different labels. The solution relies on RSVP-TE and does not require a multicast routing protocol in the service provider core.

The RFC does not specify how applications use P2MP TE LSPs or how their paths are computed.
sections.plainLanguage: A point-to-multipoint LSP carries traffic from one ingress to several egresses. Branch routers copy the data onto the paths that lead to those egresses.

sections.title: Tunnels, Sub-LSPs, and Sub-Groups
sections.content:
A P2MP tunnel is identified by a P2MP SESSION object containing a P2MP ID, Tunnel ID, and Extended Tunnel ID. The P2MP ID is a four-octet identifier unique within the ingress LSR. A P2MP LSP uses the session together with its sender address and LSP ID; each S2L sub-LSP also has a destination address.

A Path message can signal one or more S2L sub-LSPs, and multiple Path messages can describe one P2MP LSP. The SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC objects include a Sub-Group Originator ID and Sub-Group ID to distinguish those messages. These fields describe signaling state, not the data-plane branching itself.

The new S2L_SUB_LSP object has class 50. The IPv4 and IPv6 P2MP SESSION C-Types are 13 and 14; the corresponding SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC C-Types are 12 and 13.
sections.plainLanguage: The session identifies the shared tunnel, while each S2L sub-LSP identifies one destination. Sub-group fields distinguish Path messages that describe parts of the same LSP.

sections.title: Explicit Routes and Compact Path Messages
sections.content:
For a Path message with one S2L sub-LSP, an EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (ERO) can describe the route to its egress. Without an ERO, the sub-LSP uses hop-by-hop routing toward its destination.

When one Path message describes several sub-LSPs, its ERO describes the first one. A P2MP SECONDARY_EXPLICIT_ROUTE (SERO) describes each later sub-LSP from a branch LSR to its egress. Shared route portions can be inferred from the other explicit routes, avoiding repeated path information.

Every LSR processes the first route. An LSR processes a later sub-LSP when the first hop in its SERO is one of that LSR's addresses, then forwards the relevant descriptors to the downstream hops.
sections.plainLanguage: The first route is written in the main ERO. Later routes can describe only their path from a branch, which avoids repeating shared route segments.

sections.title: Setting Up Paths and Returning Reservations
sections.content:
The ingress sends Path messages for the S2L sub-LSPs. An LSR MUST process multiple Path messages for one P2MP LSP and multiple sub-LSPs in one message. If it cannot support one sub-LSP, it sends a PathErr for that sub-LSP while processing the remaining branches unless the ingress requested LSP integrity.

Each egress returns a Resv message carrying its label. An upstream node allocates its own label and does not send a Resv upstream until it has received at least one from downstream. Branch nodes SHOULD combine reservation state from several receivers, but MAY send multiple Resv messages if one would overflow.

Sub-LSPs of the same P2MP LSP on the same Resv use the same label. Different P2MP LSPs, identified by different sender addresses or LSP IDs, use different labels. If LSP integrity is requested, the reservation waits for responses from all downstream neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Path messages travel toward the egresses, and Resv messages carrying labels travel back toward the ingress. Branches can combine downstream reservations when sending them upstream.

sections.title: Adding, Removing, and Changing Destinations
sections.content:
Adding an egress is called grafting. The ingress can add sub-LSPs to an existing Path message and refresh it, or send a new Path message for only the new sub-LSPs with a new Sub-Group ID.

Removing an egress is called pruning. Implicit teardown modifies a Path or Resv message to list the sub-LSPs that remain. Explicit teardown sends a PathTear for the relevant Path message; when removing the whole P2MP LSP, the ingress MUST send a PathTear for each Path message used to signal it.

For re-optimization, the ingress can establish a new LSP using make-before-break and then remove the old one. Sub-group-based re-optimization can change only a set of sub-LSPs, but may briefly duplicate data while old and new paths coexist.
sections.plainLanguage: New destinations can be added without rebuilding every existing branch. A path can be changed by establishing its replacement before removing the old path, though some methods can briefly duplicate data.

sections.title: Branch Failures and Re-Merges
sections.content:
By default, an error on one S2L sub-LSP does not affect other sub-LSPs. The ingress can request LSP integrity by setting bit 3 of the Attributes Flags TLV. With that request, a branch failure can cause the entire P2MP LSP to fail: the branch sends PathTear messages on the other branches and reports the failure upstream.

A re-merge occurs when two branches of the same P2MP LSP meet again and share downstream outgoing interfaces. Without handling, the receiver could get duplicate data. A cross-over is similar, but the intersecting branch uses a different outgoing interface.

A node MUST support two configured approaches to re-merge: keep the re-merge and drop data from all but one incoming interface, or report the condition with PathErr so the node that created it can move the sub-LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A branch failure normally affects only its own destination. If two routes join again and would duplicate data, the node can drop one copy or signal the route that should move.

sections.title: Protection and Routers Without P2MP Support
sections.content:
Fast reroute procedures from RFC 4090 can protect P2MP LSPs in packet networks. Each S2L sub-LSP of a P2MP LSP MUST have the same protection characteristics. The RFC describes facility backup and one-to-one backup; P2MP bypass tunnels are left for further study.

An LSR that supports the signaling extensions but cannot branch in its data plane MUST report “Unable to Branch.” An LSR that does not recognize the P2MP SESSION type rejects the Path message. Older LSRs may still be transit nodes when a point-to-point LSP segment is stitched into the P2MP path; they do not process the P2MP control messages.

The security section says the extensions introduce no new security issues beyond the referenced RSVP-TE and GMPLS mechanisms. An administration can filter P2MP Path messages to limit where tunnels are established.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast-reroute methods can protect the branches. Older routers can carry traffic through a point-to-point tunnel segment, but the ingress, branch, and egress routers must support the P2MP extensions.
